paragraphs: Some questions stay open no matter how many facts you collect. Whether a true belief counts as knowledge is one. Whether it can be right to harm one person to save five is another. Philosophy is the study of questions like these, and people take it up because the answers affect how we weigh evidence and how we treat each other.

The method is argument. A philosopher states a claim, gives reasons for it and lets others test those reasons, so the course begins with that skill: reading an argument, checking whether it holds and answering it fairly. The rest applies the skill to three areas. Knowledge asks what it takes to know something and how evidence should change what we believe. Mind asks what a mind is and what makes you the same person over time. Ethics and politics look at consequences, duties, character and the agreements a society rests on.
Each lesson works through one case or thought experiment, with questions along the way and a short check at the end.
outcomes: You'll be able to set an argument out in standard form and say which premise a speaker left unstated.
You'll be able to test whether a conclusion has to follow from its premises by looking for a counterexample.
You'll be able to explain why a Gettier case, a justified true belief that is true by luck, troubles the definition of knowledge.
You'll be able to say how dualism and physicalism differ and what the Chinese Room is meant to show about minds.
You'll be able to compare what a consequentialist, a Kantian and a virtue ethicist would each say about the same moral choice.
prerequisites: You should already know what a valid argument is and how to read a truth table, as covered in Logic and Reasoning.
